query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled high-temperature substrate preheating step during LPBF of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi alloy will reduce thermal gradients, thereby minimizing residual stress, vertical cracking, and compositional segregation, and ultimately improve the mechanical integrity of the as-built parts compared to conventional LPBF without preheating.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy produced by conventional LPBF processing without substrate preheating, which typically exhibits high cooling rates leading to large thermal gradients and associated defects.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled high-temperature substrate preheating step during the LPBF process.
generation.conditions: LPBF processing of AlCrFeNiSi with comparable volumetric energy densities and layer thicknesses, ensuring the preheat temperature remains below levels that could induce unwanted phase transformations (e.g., <900 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction in temperature gradients and moderated cooling rates during solidification, leading to enhanced heterogeneous nucleation and reduced defect formation.
generation.mechanism: The elevated substrate temperature lowers the thermal gradient during melting and solidification, which reduces residual thermal stresses and slows cooling. This facilitates more uniform element distribution and minimizes the formation of vertical cracks and other defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally processed samples, LPBF parts fabricated with substrate preheating will show lower residual stress, a reduction in vertical crack density, and decreased microsegregation, thereby improving overall mechanical integrity.
generation.baseline: AlCrFeNiSi samples produced by standard LPBF without substrate preheating.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under standard LPBF operating conditions for AlCrFeNiSi using defined layer thicknesses and volumetric energy densities, provided the preheat temperature is carefully controlled to avoid promoting adverse phase changes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal preheat temperature and the exact magnitude of improvements in residual stress reduction and defect minimization are not well defined and require experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples using LPBF: one group with controlled high-temperature substrate preheating and a control group processed under ambient substrate conditions. Keep all other processing parameters identical. Evaluate the samples for residual stress (e.g., using X-ray diffraction), microstructural homogeneity and segregation (using SEM/EDS), as well as mechanical properties (via tensile and fracture toughness tests).
measurements: Defect and crack density evaluation via high-resolution microscopy
Mechanical property tests such as tensile strength and fracture toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in residual stress, vertical cracks, and microsegregation, or if their mechanical properties are not measurably enhanced compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Additive manufacturing (AM) is an emerging production technology with enormous potential to replace and supplement conventional manufacturing processes. Especially in the field of metal AM, recent developments in equipment as well as improved part quality have allowed advancements from rapid prototyping of single pieces to final part production. Among the various powder-based metal AM techniques, laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is currently the most widely used method, as it allows for higher geometrical flexibility than laser metal deposition (LMD) and higher resolution compared to electron beam melting (EBM) []. Geometrical freedom, reduced material waste, energy usage, and high degrees of automation are additional advantages of LPBF that contribute to meeting global challenges such as increased individualization, environmental friendliness, and digitalization. Furthermore, elemental segregation can be strongly reduced due to high cooling rates, which makes a large spectrum of materials processable [,,,,].

Considering this, laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is an appealing approach for manufacturing refractory metal high entropy alloys with high throughput. The intensity of modern high power laser beam sources is sufficient to effortlessly melt even tungsten []. Furthermore, small meltpool dimensions of a few hundred µm and high cooling rates in the range of 106 K/s [] during PBF-LB/M are presumed to mitigate segregation of elements during solidification which is of importance with regard to refractory metal high entropy alloys []. In addition, by adjusting the process parameters and scan strategies, the energy input can be controlled very precisely. Starting material for PBF-LB/M are metal powders. Novel alloys can be produced either by atomization of pre-alloyed powder or by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M from mixtures of commonly available elemental powders []. The later approach supports material development and high throughput investigations as the desired alloy composition can easily be produced by mixing of powder components without the need of an expensive powder atomization []. cited_evidence.text: Microsections were prepared and throughout the initial investigation, samples with noteworthy lack of fusion defects or significant keyhole porosity were ruled out. In addition to these defects, large horizontal cracks were seen as critical defects, disrupting the fabrication process due to the deterioration of the thermal conductivity towards the substrate plate, as well as the possible detachment of entire sections. Therefore, the initial set of 16 samples was reduced to four samples, which exhibited large defect-free sections, and the defects present were predominantly limited to vertical cracking (Figure 6). Vertical cracks were expected due to the absence of preheating (substrate plate preheating was not employed), coupled with the larger than usual layer thickness. Raising the build space temperature to lower cooling rates and thermal gradients is the most common approach to minimize cracking. New research also suggests that high-frequency laser power modulation is a suitable approach to prevent cracking [].
